**Recursive Subdivision:** The 3D domain is recursively divided into sub-volumes.
In standard octrees, each node has 8 children.
In pointer trees, the branching factor $N$ varies ($N^3$ children).
**Sparsity Encoding:** Empty regions are represented by null pointers or absence of children, rather than storing zero-valued voxels.
This provides compression proportional to the sparsity of the data.
**Hierarchical Traversal:** Rendering or access requires traversing from the root to the leaf.
This allows skipping large empty volumes (culling) and adapting resolution to view distance or detail requirements.
**Spatial Locality:** Children of a node are spatially contiguous.
**Subtree Merging:** The core differentiator of the DAG family is the identification of structurally identical subtrees (isomorphic nodes) and their replacement with a single shared instance.

The concept of Directed Acyclic Graphs in voxel representation emerged as a solution to the redundancy inherent in tree-based structures.

Sparse Voxel DAGs (SVDAGs) are hierarchical data structures that represent 3D voxel grids as directed acyclic graphs by merging identical subtrees into shared nodes, thereby reducing memory footprint compared to standard tree structures like Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) [S1][S2].

The evidence explicitly states that Aokana uses a 'Streaming/LOD variant of DAG' where 'subtrees only match if shape and material are identical,' which confirms the mechanism of merging identical subtrees into shared nodes. It also provides data showing significant memory reduction (424 MB VRAM vs 23 GB on disk), supporting the claim of reduced memory footprint compared to standard structures.
